current_episode.title: Late July Snacks: Nicole Bernard Dawes. Crackers and Cookies were Failing… Tortilla Chips Saved Them

guest.bio_context: Nicole Bernard Dawes is the daughter of Steve Bernard, founder of Cape Cod Potato Chips, which he started in the early 1980s and sold to Anheuser-Busch in 1985. She graduated from Tulane University in 1995, worked in the marketing and innovation department when her father bought back Cape Cod Chips in 1996 for under three million dollars, and developed the reduced-fat potato chip line before the brand was sold to Lance. After leaving Cape Cod Chips, she launched Late July Snacks in 2003 with an initial focus on organic crackers, becoming one of the first brands to launch entirely under the USDA Organic Seal.

pending_qa.q: What was the immediate market response when Late July Snacks debuted at the Natural Products Expo in Baltimore?
pending_qa.r: The company left the 2003 Natural Products Expo in Baltimore as a national brand, signing up with Whole Foods nationally and obtaining contracts with two big distributors and many other retailers. At that time, Late July was the only organic cracker brand available to natural food stores.

pending_qa.q: What challenge emerged after securing major retail orders for the newly launched organic cracker line?
pending_qa.r: While the company could manage the capital requirements for production, many retailers were excited about the organic concept but their customers did not yet understand organic products, resulting in orders from stores that probably should not have given such large orders. About two months after the Natural Products Expo show, the company's sales disappeared completely.

pending_qa.q: Why did the name 'Late July' resonate with the founder's vision for the brand?
pending_qa.r: Nicole Bernard Dawes chose Late July to represent the perfect moment in time on Cape Cod—knee deep in summer when tomatoes and corn are starting to emerge, summer vacation is in full swing, and there is a magical, special feeling. Her birthday is July 30th, which also contributed to her affinity for that time of year.

pending_qa.q: How did Nicole Bernard Dawes finance the initial launch of Late July Snacks?
pending_qa.r: She used a small amount of money from the sale of Cape Cod Chips and kept initial expenses minimal by hiring a graphic designer, covering legal fees, working without a salary herself for years, and bringing her father out of retirement to help, also without paying him a salary.

pending_qa.q: What supply chain obstacles did organic snack makers face in the early 2000s?
pending_qa.r: Even though the Organic Food Production Act had passed, there were still no established organic suppliers. There was maybe one supplier of flour, one supplier of cheese, and one supplier for each component needed, requiring founders to do extensive convincing with organic dairies and producers to source ingredients.

pending_qa.q: How did Cape Cod Potato Chips' unexpected acquisition history shape Nicole Bernard Dawes' entrepreneurial perspective?
pending_qa.r: Nicole was devastated twice when her father sold Cape Cod Chips—first to Anheuser-Busch in 1985 when she was 12 years old and considered the company like a sibling, and again in the late 1990s when he sold it to Lance for approximately 30 million dollars after buying it back in 1996 for under three million. These experiences taught her valuable lessons about business timing and helped her understand her own entrepreneurial ambitions.
